readings.title: My Ántonia excerpt: a visit to the cave (Book I, Chapter X)
readings.challenge: Notice what each person in the cave does with pride and with need, and how little the visitors understand of what they are given.
readings.focus: Help across a language and a culture: needed, given clumsily, and received with shame and anger.
readings.context: Willa Cather’s My Ántonia (1918) is told by Jim Burden, a New York lawyer remembering his boyhood in Nebraska in the 1880s, where he came as an orphan of ten to live with his grandparents and grew up near Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant family. The Shimerdas bought a poor homestead from a fellow countryman, Krajiek, and are spending their first winter in a dugout, a room cut into the bank of a draw (a shallow ravine). Jim lives with his grandparents, Josiah and Emmaline Burden, who came from Virginia; Jake Marpole and Otto Fuchs are their hired men. Mr. Shimerda is a gentle, educated man; Ambrosch is his elder son, Yulka his younger daughter, and Marek a son with a mental disability whom Jim calls “the crazy boy.” “Mamenka” is Czech for mother; ticking is strong cloth for mattresses.
readings.contentNote: Contains hunger and severe poverty, a mother’s bitter despair, and dated, demeaning words for a disabled young man.

excerpt.locator: Book I, Chapter X, the whole chapter; opens “FOR several weeks after my sleigh-ride, we heard nothing from the Shimerdas. My sore…”; closes “…were dried mushrooms. They had been gathered, probably, in some deep Bohemian forest …”.

questions.prompt: What does Mrs. Shimerda show the visitors first, and why does she seem angry rather than grateful?
facilitatorNotes: Frozen, rotting potatoes and a little flour, then an empty coffee-pot shaken “vindictive.” Her anger is the face of humiliation and of a reproach the narrator half accepts: grandmother will not admit “her own remissness” in leaving the newcomers alone so long. When the hamper comes, the anger breaks into weeping. Grandmother’s talk on the way home of being “brothers’ keepers” shows she feels it too.
evidence: shook it at us with a look positively vindictive
not admitting their stark need or her own remissness

questions.prompt: Mr. Shimerda shows Mrs. Burden the hole where his daughters sleep, then explains through Ántonia that they “were not beggars in the old country.” Why does he need to say this, and why does Ántonia insist she likes sleeping there?
facilitatorNotes: He is still “clean and neat,” with his green neckcloth and coral pin, and wants to be seen as a respectable man in hard luck, not a pauper: he had savings, lost money he did not understand, and has plans for spring. Ántonia’s cheerful “I like for sleep there” protects his pride and her family’s dignity in front of the neighbours; readers may also hear a child making the best of things.
evidence: He wanted us to know that they were not beggars in the old country
It is very cold on the floor, and this is warm like the badger hole.

questions.prompt: Grandmother throws the dried mushrooms into the stove; Jim tastes one and learns only years later what they were. What does the ending say about the visit, and about the adult narrator looking back?
facilitatorNotes: The gift was the family’s treasured food from home, given “ceremoniously,” but Mrs. Shimerda’s boast that everything is better in her country offended grandmother, who could not recognize it. Jim’s later knowledge exposes the misunderstanding, and his last image, of a deep Bohemian forest, suggests what the family left behind. Readers may still understand grandmother’s caution about food shut up with old clothes.
evidence: which the Shimerdas had brought so far and treasured so jealously, were dried mushrooms
All things for eat better in my country.

readings.title: My Ántonia excerpt: “He don’t like this kawn-tree” (Book I, Chapter XIII)
readings.challenge: Hear the quarrel between Jim and Ántonia from both sides, and notice what the older narrator lets his younger self say without correction.
readings.focus: Homesickness, envy and loyalty: two children defend their families, and a great storm closes in.
readings.context: Willa Cather’s My Ántonia (1918) is told by Jim Burden, a New York lawyer remembering his boyhood in Nebraska in the 1880s, where he came as an orphan of ten to live with his grandparents and grew up near Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant family. It is the Shimerdas’ first winter in Nebraska, spent in a dugout on a poor homestead. At Christmas the Burdens sent them gifts, and Mr. Shimerda, a gentle man who played the violin in Bohemia, came to thank them. Ambrosch is Ántonia’s elder brother. The Prince of the House of David is a popular religious novel of the time; Gladstone and Brigham Young are the hired men’s names for the bulls; dehorned cattle have had their horns removed.
readings.contentNote: Contains a boy’s hostile remarks about immigrants, and an immigrant father’s deep homesickness and sadness.

excerpt.locator: Book I, Chapter XIII, the whole chapter; opens “THE week following Christmas brought in a thaw, and by New Year’s Day all the world about…”; closes “…when it was time to begin them all over again! That was a strange, unnatural sort of day.”.

questions.prompt: Jim calls Mrs. Shimerda “a conceited, boastful old thing.” What does she do to earn it, and how does grandmother’s answer change the picture?
facilitatorNotes: She examines their furniture enviously, takes the iron pot, and says she could cook better with their things. Grandmother corrects him (“She’s not old”) and explains that poverty makes a woman grasping when her children go without. Jim reports her wisdom while still sulking; the older narrator lets both stand.
evidence: You got many, Shimerdas no got.
a body never knows what traits poverty might bring out in ’em

questions.prompt: “People who don’t like this country ought to stay at home,” Jim says. How does Ántonia answer, and what does her answer reveal about who decided the family would come?
facilitatorNotes: Her father never wanted to come: her mother made him, for land and money for the sons and husbands for the daughters, and he wept to leave his friends and their music. Ántonia then strikes back: Jim’s grandfather is rich, so why does he not help? Both children defend their own families; Jim’s remark is cruel, and Ántonia’s is not wholly fair, since the Burdens have helped. Readers can decide which hurts more.
evidence: People who don’t like this country ought to stay at home
He not want to come, nev-er!

questions.prompt: The chapter moves from the quarrel to the fighting bulls and then to the storm on Jim’s birthday. How might these scenes comment on what came before, and what might they foreshadow?
facilitatorNotes: The bulls butting across the wire mirror the families’ quarrel, and the storm subdues them both. Ántonia’s report that her father fingers his violin strings without playing, followed by “a strange, unnatural sort of day,” darkens the end. Some readers will see only farm life; others will feel a warning in the snow and the silence of the violin.
evidence: Some days he take his violin out of his box and make with his fingers on the strings
That was a strange, unnatural sort of day.

readings.title: My Ántonia excerpt: a horse-collar and a cow (Book I, Chapter XVIII)
readings.challenge: Follow a feud from start to finish, and decide who in it behaves best and why.
readings.focus: How neighbours quarrel and make peace across language and custom, and what young Jim does and does not learn from it.
readings.context: Willa Cather’s My Ántonia (1918) is told by Jim Burden, a New York lawyer remembering his boyhood in Nebraska in the 1880s, where he came as an orphan of ten to live with his grandparents and grew up near Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant family. In the family’s first winter Mr. Shimerda took his own life, and his elder son Ambrosch, about nineteen, became head of the family. Ántonia, about fifteen, now works in the fields and no longer has lessons; Jim, now eleven, has started at the country school. Jake and Otto are the Burdens’ hired men; Jim’s grandfather had sold the Shimerdas a cow on credit. A horse-collar is the padded ring of a harness; a justice of the peace is a local magistrate; a cultivator is a horse-drawn tool for weeding between rows; colic is a dangerous bellyache in horses; masses are Catholic services that may be offered for the souls of the dead.
readings.contentNote: Contains a fistfight, profanity, prejudiced generalizations about foreigners, dated language about a young man with a mental disability, and a girl’s passing threat to drown herself.

excerpt.locator: Book I, Chapter XVIII, the whole chapter; opens “AFTER I began to go to the country school, I saw less of the Bohemians. We were sixteen…”; closes “…disconcerted. “Have the last word, mam,” he said cheerfully. “It’s a lady’s privilege.””.

questions.prompt: Who starts the fight between Jake and Ambrosch? How does each side tell the story afterwards?
facilitatorNotes: Ambrosch returns the collar ruined and turns his back; Jake yanks him off the ladder; Ambrosch kicks; Jake knocks him down. Afterwards Jake decides “These foreigners ain’t the same,” Jim that they are “all like Krajiek and Ambrosch underneath,” and the Shimerdas that Jake had to sell his pig to pay his fine. Each side keeps the version that flatters it.
evidence: These foreigners ain’t the same.
Jake-y, Jake-y, sell the pig and pay the slap!

questions.prompt: Grandfather is “never a party” to the feud. What does he do instead, and what do his actions suggest about how to treat neighbours you disagree with?
facilitatorNotes: He has Jake pay his fine before trouble can start, rides out himself to save the sick horse, defends Ambrosch’s gift to the priest against grandmother’s objection, offers the family paid work, and forgives the debt on the cow. He is practical, tolerant and generous, and judges people by what their actions show they believe.
evidence: If he can spare six dollars, pinched as he is, it shows he believes what he professes.
Pay no more, keep cow.

questions.prompt: When Mrs. Shimerda kisses grandfather’s hand, Jim says it “seemed to bring the Old World very close.” What does he mean? Is the chapter’s comedy at her expense fair?
facilitatorNotes: Kissing a landowner’s hand is how a European peasant thanks a lord; it shows how much the cow means and how sure she was of losing it. The narrator tells her attempt to hide the cow in the bank as “a funny sight,” but her fear was real. Readers can weigh the affection and the condescension in Jim’s portrait, and notice that her parting joke about the pig gives her the last word.
evidence: Somehow, that seemed to bring the Old World very close.
she was trying to hide the cow in an old cave in the bank

readings.title: My Ántonia excerpt: a storm from the chicken-house roof (Book I, Chapter XIX)
readings.challenge: Read the storm slowly, image by image, and connect it with the conversation that ends Book I.
readings.focus: A summer of happiness at harvest, and Ántonia’s clear sense that her life and Jim’s will be different.
readings.context: Willa Cather’s My Ántonia (1918) is told by Jim Burden, a New York lawyer remembering his boyhood in Nebraska in the 1880s, where he came as an orphan of ten to live with his grandparents and grew up near Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant family. This is the last chapter of Book I. After her father’s death Ántonia, about fifteen, works in the fields for her brother Ambrosch; a quarrel between the families has just been made up, and Jim’s grandfather has hired Ántonia to help in the kitchen during the wheat harvest. Fertilizing here means pollinating; heat lightning is distant lightning without thunder; a quay is a stone landing-place for ships.

excerpt.locator: Book I, Chapter XIX, the whole chapter, ending Book I; opens “JULY came on with that breathless, brilliant heat which makes the plains of Kansas and…”; closes “…like you, that is different. Things will be easy for you. But they will be hard for us.””.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator imagine the plain “under glass,” and what does his grandfather foresee about the cornfields?
facilitatorNotes: The weather is as perfect for corn as a greenhouse. Grandfather foresees that the scattered fields will become “the world’s cornfields,” one of the great economic facts that underlie peace and war. The older narrator knows he was right; a family’s field is already part of a world economy.
evidence: If all the great plain from the Missouri to the Rocky Mountains had been under glass
not the Shimerdas’ cornfields, or Mr. Bushy’s, but the world’s cornfields

questions.prompt: Ántonia says, “I like to be like a man.” What has field work given her, and what does it cost her in other people’s eyes?
facilitatorNotes: Strength, pride and joy in being out of doors: she asks Jim to feel her muscles. Grandmother thinks it makes her unwomanly, and Jim has resented her toughness and her imitation of Ambrosch. Readers may hear freedom in her claim, or necessity making the best of itself.
evidence: I not care that your grandmother say it makes me like a man.
Why do you all the time try to be like Ambrosch?

questions.prompt: The sky looks “like the quay of some splendid sea-coast city, doomed to destruction,” and one small cloud drifts west “unattended.” How do these images prepare for Ántonia’s last words in Book I?
facilitatorNotes: The splendour is threatened, and the lone cloud moves away on its own, as the two friends’ lives will. Ántonia wishes her father had lived to see the summer, then answers Jim plainly: things will be easy for him and hard for her family. She sees class and circumstance clearly where Jim sees only her moods.
evidence: like the quay of some splendid sea-coast city, doomed to destruction
Things will be easy for you. But they will be hard for us.

readings.title: My Ántonia excerpt: moving to Black Hawk (Book II, Chapter I)
readings.challenge: Notice what the move to town ends and what it begins, for each character.
readings.focus: Leaving the farm: friends lost without ceremony, a boy remade by town, and Ántonia hired out like a man.
readings.context: Willa Cather’s My Ántonia (1918) is told by Jim Burden, a New York lawyer remembering his boyhood in Nebraska in the 1880s, where he came as an orphan of ten to live with his grandparents and grew up near Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant family. Book II, “The Hired Girls,” begins when Jim is thirteen. In Book I the Burdens’ hired men, Jake Marpole and Otto Fuchs, ran the farm and looked after Jim like older brothers; Ántonia’s father died in the family’s first winter, and her brother Ambrosch now runs their farm. Sharpers are swindlers; “keeps” is a game of marbles played for keeps; thrashers (threshers) separate grain from straw; to husk corn is to strip the ears by hand.

excerpt.locator: Book II, “The Hired Girls,” Chapter I, the whole chapter; opens “I HAD been living with my grandfather for nearly three years when he decided to move to…”; closes “…saved her from this by getting her a place to work with our neighbors, the Harlings.”.

questions.prompt: How does Jim part from Jake and Otto, and why might the narrator tell their leaving so briefly?
facilitatorNotes: They go “without warning,” in their Sunday clothes, and he never sees them again; his letter comes back “unclaimed.” The plain, short telling makes the loss real: people who gave him what “cannot be bought” simply pass out of his life, as people did on the frontier.
evidence: had given us things that cannot be bought in any market in the world
and I never saw them again

questions.prompt: Jim says he was “quite another boy, or thought I was.” What does town teach him, and what keeps him in check?
facilitatorNotes: He learns to fight, play “keeps,” tease and swear, and only Mrs. Harling’s watchfulness keeps him within bounds. The phrase “or thought I was” is the older narrator smiling at a boy who believed a few new tricks had changed him.
evidence: I was quite another boy, or thought I was
I was restrained from utter savagery only by the fact that Mrs. Harling, our nearest neighbor, kept an eye on me

questions.prompt: Ambrosch hires his sister out “like a man.” Why do the farmers prefer her to him, and who decides where she goes next? What does this suggest about Ántonia’s freedom?
facilitatorNotes: She works hard and is liked; they would rather have her “for a hand than Ambrosch.” Her brother takes her wages and decides her work; grandmother then arranges a place for her with the Harlings. Kind or not, other people make every decision. Readers may debate whether going into service in town rescues her or only changes who directs her.
evidence: Ambrosch hired his sister out like a man
said they would rather have her for a hand than Ambrosch

readings.title: My Ántonia excerpt: the Harlings (Book II, Chapter II)
readings.challenge: Compare how the narrator presents Mrs. Harling, her husband and Frances, and notice what the Harlings decide about Ántonia before she arrives.
readings.focus: A household of strong women, and a bargain about a girl’s wages made over her head.
readings.context: Willa Cather’s My Ántonia (1918) is told by Jim Burden, a New York lawyer remembering his boyhood in Nebraska in the 1880s, where he came as an orphan of ten to live with his grandparents and grew up near Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant family. Jim, now thirteen, lives in the prairie town of Black Hawk with his grandparents. Ántonia, about seventeen, has worked on neighbouring farms for her brother Ambrosch since their father’s death. Christiania is the old name of Oslo, Norway; grain elevators are tall storehouses for grain beside the railway; Annapolis is the United States Naval Academy; Wick Cutter is the town’s money-lender.

excerpt.locator: Book II, Chapter II, the whole chapter; opens “GRANDMOTHER often said that if she had to live in town, she thanked God she lived next…”; closes “…she’ll forget those things,” said Mrs. Harling confidently, as we rose to take our leave.”.

questions.prompt: What makes Mrs. Harling “like her house”? Find the details that make her energy felt.
facilitatorNotes: She is short, square and sturdy; her footsteps shake her floors; wash-day is interesting, preserving-time a festival, house-cleaning “like a revolution,” and her laugh is quick and intelligent. The house and the woman are both solid, busy and warm.
evidence: Mrs. Harling was short and square and sturdy-looking, like her house.
house-cleaning was like a revolution

questions.prompt: Mr. Harling is “stern and exacting” with Frances and “very indulgent” with Charley. What does the contrast suggest, and how does Frances use her gifts?
facilitatorNotes: Frances, the able one, works without holidays; Charley, who has no interest in business, is given guns and tools and asked nothing. The father rewards the son and taxes the daughter. Frances turns her business knowledge into care for the farmers, carrying them in her mind “as if they were characters in a book or a play,” as Jim himself does with the people of his story.
evidence: Because of her unusual business ability, he was stern and exacting with her.
She carried them all in her mind as if they were characters in a book or a play.

questions.prompt: Who speaks for Ántonia in the bargain over her wages, and how do the Harlings describe her? How confident should we be in Mrs. Harling’s last line?
facilitatorNotes: Ambrosch wants every cent paid to him; Mrs. Harling insists on keeping fifty dollars a year for Ántonia’s own use, and Mrs. Shimerda offers geese “to make even.” Ántonia herself is not present. The Harlings praise her looks warmly. Mrs. Harling’s certainty that the girl will be happy and “forget those things” is generous, but it assumes a past can simply be forgotten; readers can judge whether that is kindness or overconfidence.
evidence: she would keep fifty dollars a year for Ántonia’s own use
The girl will be happy here, and she’ll forget those things

readings.title: My Ántonia excerpt: Ántonia at the Harlings’ (Book II, Chapter III)
readings.challenge: Watch how Jim describes the people he admires and the people he resents, and notice where his jealousy shows.
readings.focus: A new home for Ántonia, and a household that changes when the father is in it.
readings.context: Willa Cather’s My Ántonia (1918) is told by Jim Burden, a New York lawyer remembering his boyhood in Nebraska in the 1880s, where he came as an orphan of ten to live with his grandparents and grew up near Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant family. Ántonia, about seventeen, has come to work as cook and maid for the Harlings, the Burdens’ neighbours in Black Hawk; Jim is about thirteen. Charley is the Harlings’ only son and Nina the youngest child; Mr. Harling is a grain merchant often away on business. An ell is a wing built at right angles to a house; the “nobles” are the landowners Ántonia remembers from Bohemia.
readings.contentNote: Contains a passing, dated reference to minstrel shows, in which white performers mocked Black people.

excerpt.locator: Book II, Chapter III, the whole chapter; opens “ON Saturday Ambrosch drove up to the back gate, and Ántonia jumped down from the wagon…”; closes “…and neatly over the keys, her eyes fixed on the music with intelligent concentration.”.

questions.prompt: Ántonia hopes she will be “the kind of girl you like better, now I come to town.” What does she want, and what does Mrs. Harling find to be her “greatest fault”?
facilitatorNotes: She wants approval and a new start, and arrives in shoes and stockings. Her fault is stopping work to play with the children: the warmth that makes her loved is the thing a mistress must correct. She learns English so fast that by autumn she speaks like the rest of them.
evidence: Maybe I be the kind of girl you like better, now I come to town
Her greatest fault, Mrs. Harling found, was that she so often stopped her work and fell to playing with the children.

questions.prompt: Jim admits he was “jealous” of Charley. How does that jealousy colour what he tells us about Charley and about Nina?
facilitatorNotes: Charley’s skill and Ántonia’s devotion to him (“a sort of prince”) are reported with an edge; Nina’s tears win every quarrel, and Jim confesses he “often wanted to shake her.” The adult narrator is candid about a boy’s envy, which invites us to read his other judgments carefully too.
evidence: I was jealous of Tony’s admiration for Charley Harling.
but I often wanted to shake her

questions.prompt: How does the house change when Mr. Harling is home, and why does Jim imagine the “nobles” of Bohemia looking like him?
facilitatorNotes: The children are sent to bed or out of the house, and his wife gives him all her attention; even his shadow on the blind seems “arrogant.” Unlike other Black Hawk fathers he seems “autocratic and imperial,” so Jim links him with Old World aristocrats. Readers may see Mrs. Harling’s devotion as loyalty or as the price of living with power.
evidence: it seemed to me an arrogant shadow
Mr. Harling, therefore, seemed to me autocratic and imperial in his ways.

readings.title: My Ántonia excerpt: Lena Lingard comes to town (Book II, Chapters IV–V)
readings.challenge: Weigh what the Harlings, the Norwegian settlement and Jim say about Lena against what she says and does herself.
readings.focus: A girl with a reputation: gossip, judgment, and Lena’s own plain account of her life.
readings.context: Willa Cather’s My Ántonia (1918) is told by Jim Burden, a New York lawyer remembering his boyhood in Nebraska in the 1880s, where he came as an orphan of ten to live with his grandparents and grew up near Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant family. Ántonia, about seventeen, works for the Harlings in Black Hawk, and Jim, about fourteen, lives next door. Lena Lingard is the eldest daughter of a poor Norwegian farmer near the Shimerdas. Findings are a dressmaker’s small supplies; “to ask lief” is to ask permission; the Burlington is the railway; commercial travelers are salesmen, and Marshall Field’s is a Chicago store; “retail trade” means a shopkeeper. The rhyme at the head of Chapter IV is from a children’s singing game. Squaw Creek is the creek’s historical name, which uses a slur for a Native American woman.
readings.contentNote: Contains gossip about a teenage girl and a married man, a mentally ill woman’s threats with a corn-knife, dated language about mental illness, and a place name that uses an ethnic slur.

excerpt.locator: Book II, Chapters IV and V, both whole chapters; opens ““I won’t have none of your weevily wheat, and I won’t have none of your barley, But I’ll…”; closes “…for them, all the same,” she murmured, as if she were answering some remembered reproach.”.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Harling and Frances receive Lena differently. What does each say, and what is Mrs. Harling worried about?
facilitatorNotes: Mrs. Harling speaks “severely” and “skeptically,” warns her about dances and about girls working in hotels; Frances teases her kindly and invites her back. Mrs. Harling fears for a pretty country girl’s reputation and safety in town; Frances is readier to judge Lena by how she behaves now.
evidence: See that you don’t forget to
if you’ll only keep your head and not go gadding about to dances all the time

questions.prompt: The settlement blamed Lena for Ole Benson’s behaviour. What does the story actually show her doing, and how does she answer Mrs. Shimerda? Notice also how Jim describes her.
facilitatorNotes: Ole wandered off to sit where she herded; she came to church in a borrowed dress; he lifted her onto her horse; his wife chased her with a corn-knife. Lena says she never encouraged him and cannot order him off: “It ain’t my prairie.” The community blames the girl rather than the married man. Jim’s own description, which dwells on how undressed her white legs and arms make her seem, shows that he looks at her the way the town does.
evidence: I can’t help it if he hangs around, and I can’t order him off. It ain’t my prairie.
which somehow made her seem more undressed than other girls who went scantily clad

questions.prompt: Lena says she wants no husband and wants to help her mother. How does the scene with her brother Chris and the handkerchiefs support or complicate the town’s view of her?
facilitatorNotes: Lena wants work that will let her support her family without asking anyone’s leave. In the store she helps Chris choose B for Berthe, because “Nobody ever calls her by it now,” seeing her mother as a person with a name; then she cries, homesick. The scene shows a loyal, tender daughter, not the flirt the gossip describes; readers may also notice that she likes pretty things and the hotel’s gaiety, and that both can be true.
evidence: I want to be so I can help my mother and the children at home, and not have to ask lief of anybody.
Nobody ever calls her by it now.

readings.title: My Ántonia excerpt: winter, and a story about a tramp (Book II, Chapter VI)
readings.challenge: Follow the chapter from a bleak town to a warm kitchen to a disturbing story, and notice how each listener responds.
readings.focus: Light against winter, and a story of despair told among children by someone who loves life.
readings.context: Willa Cather’s My Ántonia (1918) is told by Jim Burden, a New York lawyer remembering his boyhood in Nebraska in the 1880s, where he came as an orphan of ten to live with his grandparents and grew up near Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant family. Ántonia works as cook for the Harlings in Black Hawk; Jim, about fourteen, lives next door. Mrs. Harling plays and explains operas for the children (Martha, Norma and Rigoletto were popular ones); charades are acting games. A Laplander is a Sámi, of the reindeer-herding people of the far north; a crèche is a Christmas nativity scene; a freshet is a sudden flood. At threshing, a band-cutter on the machine’s deck cuts the twine round each sheaf before it goes in; “The Old Oaken Bucket” is a sentimental American poem about a childhood home.
readings.contentNote: Ántonia tells of a tramp who killed himself by jumping into a threshing machine; the death is described briefly but directly.

excerpt.locator: Book II, Chapter VI, the whole chapter; opens “WINTER comes down savagely over a little town on the prairie. The wind that sweeps in…”; closes “…imagine Ántonia’s living for a week in any other house in Black Hawk than the Harlings’.”.

questions.prompt: In the winter sunset the wind seems to say that summer’s beauty was “lies.” How does the rest of the opening answer that bleak voice?
facilitatorNotes: People hunger for colour: the children linger by the church’s crude stained glass, and the Harlings’ lit windows draw Jim “like the painted glass.” Warmth, music and colour are what people make against winter’s “truth.” Readers can argue whether the wind speaks truth or only a mood.
evidence: This is reality, whether you like it or not.
In the winter bleakness a hunger for color came over people

questions.prompt: What do the tramp’s words and the things in his pocket suggest about him? Why might Cather leave him unexplained?
facilitatorNotes: He jokes about ponds too low to drown in, sneers that the harvest hands are Norwegians (“I thought this was Americy”), and carries a penknife, a wishbone and a worn copy of a poem about a childhood home. No name, no past: he stands for the homeless and despairing whom the settlers’ story of hope leaves out. Some readers will connect his homesickness with Mr. Shimerda’s.
evidence: nothing but an old penknife in his pocket and the wishbone of a chicken wrapped up in a piece of paper, and some poetry
I thought this was Americy.

questions.prompt: Ántonia asks, “What would anybody want to kill themselves in summer for?” What does the question reveal about her, and why does the narrator follow it with the “basic harmony” between her and Mrs. Harling?
facilitatorNotes: She loves summer and harvest work so much that despair in that season makes no sense to her. Mrs. Harling turns the talk back to the taffy, and the narrator praises what the two women share: strong natures and “a relish of life” that answers death with warmth and work. Some readers find that answer too quick; others find it wise in a kitchen full of children.
evidence: What would anybody want to kill themselves in summer for?
Deep down in each of them there was a kind of hearty joviality, a relish of life

readings.title: My Ántonia excerpt: Blind d’Arnault at the Boys’ Home (Book II, Chapter VII)
readings.challenge: Read a portrait of a musician critically: separate what the chapter shows d’Arnault doing from the racist stereotypes through which the narrator describes him.
readings.focus: Music, freedom and the hired girls’ first dance, seen through a narrator whose racial assumptions distort what he sees.
readings.context: Willa Cather’s My Ántonia (1918) is told by Jim Burden, a New York lawyer remembering his boyhood in Nebraska in the 1880s, where he came as an orphan of ten to live with his grandparents and grew up near Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant family. Jim, about fourteen, lives in the prairie town of Black Hawk; Ántonia works for the Harlings, and her friends Lena Lingard and Tiny Soderball also work in town. The Boys’ Home is the town hotel, run by Mrs. Gardener while her husband Johnnie keeps the desk; the guests are travelling salesmen. Blind d’Arnault is a touring Black pianist; Cather is generally thought to have drawn on Thomas Wiggins, “Blind Tom,” a musical prodigy born into slavery and exhibited for profit. “Mulatto” is a period word for a person of mixed Black and white ancestry; “My Old Kentucky Home” is a Stephen Foster song written for the minstrel stage; Booth and Barrett and Mary Anderson were famous actors of the day.
readings.contentNote: This chapter describes Blind d’Arnault, a Black pianist, through the racist stereotypes and slurs of Cather’s time: demeaning descriptions of his body, voice and mother, and generalizations about Black people. It also mentions slavery, a blind child being beaten, and a white woman’s face called “Indian-like.” The words are the narrator’s and the author’s, kept as written for critical reading, not endorsed.

excerpt.locator: Book II, Chapter VII, the whole chapter; opens “WINTER lies too long in country towns; hangs on until it is stale and shabby, old and…”; closes “…gate, whispering in the cold until the restlessness was slowly chilled out of us.”.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Harling has known d’Arnault for years, and Mrs. Gardener has the piano tuned before he comes. What do these details, and the story of the child Samson at Miss Nellie’s piano, show about his gift and how he won it?
facilitatorNotes: People who know music respect him. As a blind child he crept to the piano again and again although he was beaten and threatened with the mastiff, taught himself from what he overheard, and proved to have absolute pitch and a remarkable memory. The story is one of courage and hunger for music against fear and shame.
evidence: Mrs. Gardener, she always has this piano tuned up before I come.
They found he had absolute pitch, and a remarkable memory.

questions.prompt: Jim hears in d’Arnault’s voice “the note of docile subservience,” and calls him a prodigy who played “barbarously and wonderfully.” What is wrong with descriptions like these, and how do they clash with what the chapter itself shows?
facilitatorNotes: They are racist stereotypes of Cather’s era: the contented servant, the pseudo-science about head shape, the idea that Black musicians played by instinct rather than mind. They turn a person into a type. The chapter’s own evidence contradicts them: his discipline and memory, his ear (he hears the girls’ “little feet” through a wall), his command of a room of white men, his career as far as a Russian nobleman. Jim’s nostalgia for the Virginia of his childhood shapes what he sees. Many readers find that Cather admires the genius while degrading the man; a strong answer names both and quotes the narrator’s words as his assumptions, not as facts.
evidence: with the note of docile subservience in it
He was always a negro prodigy who played barbarously and wonderfully.

questions.prompt: D’Arnault hears the girls dancing and plays for them until his manager shuts the piano. What does this night mean to the hired girls, and why can Jim and Ántonia not bring themselves to go to bed?
facilitatorNotes: With Mrs. Gardener away, the hired girls, who were dancing alone in the dining-room, are pulled into the parlour and dance with the salesmen: a first taste of the freedom and admiration that town can offer. The older narrator’s sigh over their “light of youth” suggests he knows what became of it. The excitement keeps Jim and Ántonia whispering at the gate; readers may notice that the musician whom Jim describes so condescendingly is the one who sets them all free for an evening.
evidence: Now, you girls, you ain’t goin’ to let that floor get cold?
We were so excited that we dreaded to go to bed.
